newsitem.title: USA: Jewish group demands restitution from Swiss.
newsitem.headline: Jewish group demands restitution from Swiss.

text.p: Switzerland's admission that it struck a secret deal 47 years ago to give Poland wealth unclaimed from Swiss banks after the Second World War sparked a firestorm of protest on Friday and one Jewish group claimed Switzerland owed Holocaust victims millions of dollars.

Meanwhile, the office of Senate Banking Committee Chairman Alfonse D'Amato said Switzerland was wrong in continuing to deny that the deal opened the way for its citizens to receive millions of dollars in compensation from Poland for Swiss property seized in the then-Communist country.

The New York Republican's office released a 1950 statement from Switzerland's then-foreign minister saying the heirless property of Polish citizens in Switzerland was to be deposited in a Swiss bank account for the Polish National Bank and that the Polish government had agreed to take over the obligations it owed Swiss citizens, banks and life insurance companies.

It said the statement was found in the archives of the American Jewish Distribution Committee, which in 1949 tried to publicise the secret agreements in the hopes of stopping them from going into effect.

Switzerland acknowledged on Friday that it struck a confidential deal with Poland in 1949 to liquidate Polish citizens' unclaimed wealth. Jewish groups maintain most of that belonged to Holocaust victims who had used Switzerland as a safe haven to protect their wealth from the Nazis.

Kalman Sultanik, a vice president of the World Jewish Congress, said the Swiss admission proved that the Swiss "immorally transferred Jewish assets to Poland" and he demanded that the Swiss pay millions of dollars in compensation to the World Jewish Restitution Organisation.

He said the admission was a major reversal of a position the Swiss adamantly held since 1949 and threw into question the validity of Switzerland's 1946 treaty with Britain, France and the United States on the disposition of unclaimed wealth in Swiss banks. The agreement called for half of the unclaimed assets to go to the Allies to use to help war victims.

The three allies had filed a diplomatic protest against Switzerland in 1949 over the secret deal but the Swiss denied that it had taken place. The deal was detailed in an exchange of letters dated June 25, 1949 that accompanied a Swiss-Polish agreement on compensation for nationalised property.

The agreement publicly called for Poland to pay Switzerland 52.1 million Swiss francs ($41 million at 1996 rates). But the foreign ministry adamantly denied the deal let Switzerland keep Holocaust victims' riches for itself.

"Various sides alleged yesterday that Switzerland struck a secret accord with Poland after World War II that let Switzerland seize for itself dormant assets of Polish citizens. This allegation is wrong," the ministry said.

Switzerland also struck post-war compensation accords with Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, Romania and Hungary, it said. D'Amato's office has said it believes these accords also contained similar secret agreements on heirless property.
